newsitem.title: USA: Centennial to issue findings on internal probe.
newsitem.headline: Centennial to issue findings on internal probe.

text.p: Centennial Technologies Inc. said Wednesday a special committee of its board of directors investigating alleged fraud by the company's founder will release some findings before the stock market opens on Thursday.
Centennial's stock, rattled by allegations of insider trading against its founder and former chief executive, was halted all day Wednesday by the New York Stock Exchange pending the news.
The company's treasurer, Don Peck, declined to elaborate on the statement.
"I really can't comment on anything except look for a press release tonight or tomorrow," he said. "We're getting spanked for saying anything to the press."
The Billerica, Mass.-based manufacturer of personal computer memory cards said the special committee would meet late Wednesday to examine the interim results of its internal investigation.

The company formed the committee earlier this month after it fired founder and Chief Executive Emanuel Pinez after he admitted to the board he falsified Centennial's sales to meet Wall Street expectations, according to court documents.
Pinez was charged by the SEC and the U.S. Attorney's office in Boston with insider trading and has been held the last 13 days in a Plymouth, Mass. jail.
Chief Financial Officer James Murphy also was relieved of his duties and was assisting Centennial in its investigation, the company said.

Some of its financial statements appeared to have been falsified, the company said, and it expected to have to restate its earnings for 1996 and the first half of 1997 to report a loss for those periods rather than profits.
Pinez's lawyer, Robert Ullmann, has denied his client engaged in any wrongdoing.

Centennial's stock tripled in value on Tuesday, surging $10.25 to $14.75 after Lawrence Ramaekers, the interim chief executive to replace Pinez, told Reuters the company had record sales last week despite news of a financial scandal.
When asked during the interview to clarify, he said; "I think so, I don't have the numbers with me, but that's what I've been told this morning."

The company later downplayed those remarks, saying that Ramaekers "intended to convey that Centennial is continuing to build and sell its product and he was pleased by customer confidence that continued orders confirmed."
Centennial's stock, which hit a low of $1.75 last week, has been popular among retail investors and has hardly been covered by Wall Street analysts.
The president of a retail brokerage firm which had recommended Centennial to retail investors said he "wouldn't expect any stock to have that kind of turbulence. I've never seen anything like it."
The broker, who declined to be identified, wondered why the New York Stock Exchange, which will delist the stock on March 3, ever allowed it to trade again.
"I dont think the stock exchange should have opened it until they had material information," he said. "I hate to see customers beaten up like this."
